data.title: Vampires in Great Moravia – anti-vampire burials from Modrá
data.excerpt: Two of the inhumation graves examined at Modrá near Velehrad depart sharply from the usual early medieval burial rite: one child had a pelvic bone clamped between its jaws, the other a skull pierced by a stone. Moravian archaeologists call them vampire graves, and a third case — a body with the head removed and weighted down with eleven stones — comes from inside the sanctuary at the Skalka nad Váhom hillfort.
data.metaTitle: Vampires in Great Moravia: the graves from Modrá
data.metaDescription: Two unusual inhumation graves from Modrá near Velehrad show an anti-vampire burial rite. A third case comes from the Skalka nad Váhom hillfort.

children.text: In recent years several inhumation graves have been examined at Modrá near Velehrad (the Uherské Hradiště agglomeration). Two of them, however, depart from the usual burial rite. Moravian archaeologists write about the two most recent vampire finds in the information leaflet „Raně středověké hroby vampírú z Modré u Velehradu“ (Early Medieval Vampire Graves from Modrá near Velehrad), which I take the liberty of quoting:

blocks.text:
Grave 1 / 2002

The grave was discovered in the course of a rescue archaeological excavation, on the area of the future archaeological open-air museum. The remains took the form of an incomplete skeleton in an extended supine position oriented NW–SE, of which the long bones of the lower limbs, the skull resting on the right temple, the greater part of the left pelvis, the ribs of the left half of the trunk, the left scapula and the left humerus lay in their original position. Variously dislocated were the vertebrae, which lay partly behind the skull and partly on the left side of the chest, while some were even found in the fill above the skeleton. The entire upper part of the right pelvic bone, that is, the blade of the ilium, was firmly clamped between the lower and upper jaws of the buried individual! The bones of the feet and hands did not survive, and the right scapula and the right clavicle were not found either. According to the determination of the anthropologist Marta Dočkalová of the Moravian Museum, the skeletal remains from the grave belonged to a child of about 6 years of age (age category Infans I-II). The grave contained no finds. The individual buried in the grave — a small child — was laid in a plain, shallow pit without any grave goods and without any surviving parts of clothing. It is also clear, however, that the grave, or rather the bodily remains of the child lying in it, were subsequently exposed to a secondary intervention. The question arises as to who caused that secondary intervention.

At the same time we believe that whoever it was resolved upon it only after a certain interval from the time at which the burial act took place. Only in that way was it possible to avoid a certain "morbidity" which would necessarily have accompanied the dislocation of the bones, especially the removal and subsequent insertion of the blade of the ilium between the teeth, had the body of the buried child still held well "together".
blocks.author: Luděk Galuška, Miroslav Vaškových
blocks.source: information leaflet: Raně středověké hroby vampírů z Modré u Velehradu

blocks.text:
Grave 1 / 2010

The grave was discovered in April 2010 in a trench dug for the laying of a low-voltage cable. Below the ground surface a conspicuous cluster of large sandstone blocks of irregular shape was first discovered. After the cluster of stones had been partly dismantled, it became apparent that for the most part they covered a grave pit. In it, in an extended position, lay the incomplete and poorly preserved skeleton of a juvenile individual. Only the long bones of the lower limbs and the skull survived in relatively good condition. The frontal bone of the skull of the buried individual had been pierced by a large angular stone, which was still contained in it at the time the grave was uncovered. According to the anthropologist Jana Langová of the Museum of South-East Moravia in Zlín, the skeleton in the grave belonged to a child who died at the age of 8-9 (age category Infans II). The injury to the skull, caused by a blow with a large stone, corresponds to a post-mortem intervention. Otherwise no further traces of violent intervention, injuries or pathological manifestations or changes were found on the bones. Beneath the skull a typical Great Moravian bronze earring was discovered, originally perhaps with a single basket pendant. The grave was probably planned from the very outset with the purpose that a "dangerous" individual would be laid in it.

Data on the age of the graves

Both graves can be dated at the earliest to the Early Middle Ages, that is, to the time of Great Moravia or to the period immediately following it, i.e. to the 9th and the first half of the 10th century. Let us add that the dating of the graves to the 9th and the first half of the 10th century is contradicted neither by the orientation of the grave pits, or rather the position of the deceased, which with slight deviations follows a W–E direction, nor by the find of the typical bronze earring.

Interpretation

As we have already indicated, graves 1 / 2002 and 1 / 2010 in no way fit, by their character, into the framework of ordinary burial in the Early Middle Ages. This is chiefly because the skeletal remains of the two small children buried in them bear clear traces of violent intervention on the part of the survivors. On the basis of the interventions described, the children buried in both graves may be regarded as "vampires". From the point of view of early medieval people, and indeed from that of people today, these were representatives of the most dangerous form of revenant, that is, a buried individual with the possibility of returning to the world of the living, who was credited with the ability to rise at night and go to suck the blood of people and animals alike, and further to cause various epidemics and many other calamities.

Conclusion

Graves 1 / 2002 and 1 / 2010 from Modrá near Velehrad substantially add to our insights into the burial rite of the old Slavs in the Early Middle Ages. Both were evidently buried in the period of the final existence of the Great Moravian state or in the time immediately following, that is, between the close of the 9th century and the middle of the 10th. There is no doubt that the belief in vampires is as old as humanity itself. It was a belief deeply rooted among people for ages, one whose associated practices, sometimes of a very harsh and even morbid character, were not restricted, let alone halted, even by the Catholic Church. In some parts of the world these practices are applied to this day.
blocks.author: Luděk Galuška, Miroslav Vaškových
blocks.source: information leaflet: Raně středověké hroby vampírů z Modré u Velehradu

I add to this topic a Slovak vampire too, from the hillfort of
A vampire in the sanctuary at the hillfort

All the circumstances concerning the small church found at the hillfort remain a mystery to this day. Was it then of stone, or of wood? Does it date from the time of Great Moravia, or was it built only during the development of sacral architecture in the Kingdom of Hungary? Was it a Christian building at all, or did a pagan temple originally stand here, which survived in the awareness of the common people as the „Temple of Venus“ mentioned at the beginning? Why would anyone build a church at a hillfort which bears several marks of a rather refuge-like character, when a few kilometres from Skalka there was a central hillfort on the site of today's Trenčín castle? One of the greatest mysteries, however, remains the vampire's grave located inside the sanctuary.

The case of the individual from the grave placed in the interior of the sacral feature at the hillfort in Skalka nad Váhom might at first sight recall the application of the principle enshrined in the „Legis Salicae“, according to which a sacral building was to be erected over the grave of an important individual. The deceased from the interior of the sanctuary at the Skalka hillfort, however, can hardly have belonged among the more important individuals of the time, because
anti-vampire practices were carried out on him, including the subsequent removal of the head and the weighting down of the upper part of the trunk with eleven stones

. As has been mentioned, the skeleton lacked the skull together with five cervical vertebrae; these had been removed from the grave subsequently. Manifestations of this kind in our region are termed posterior anti-vampire practices, and they were carried out chiefly at non-church cemeteries with several lingering manifestations of the pagan rite. From the milieu of Great Moravia we know of several cases of so-called vampire graves, in which individuals were, for ritual reasons, mutilated after death or rather after burial, especially by the removal of one of the limbs or of the head, or were weighted down with large boulders. The purpose of these practices may have been, for example, the endeavour to ensure that the deceased could not rise from the grave and work evil upon the living.
